name: Fitts's law
summary: The time to hit a target depends on its distance and its size.
when: Any screen with controls a user clicks or taps.

rule.template: Make every interactive element at least {minPx} by {minPx}.

source: Fitts, P. M. (1954). The information capacity of the human motor system in controlling the amplitude of movement.

name: Hick's law
summary: The time it takes to decide grows with the number of choices.
when: Screens where the user picks one action from several.

rule.template: Limit primary actions to {max} per screen.

source: Hick, W. E. (1952). On the rate of gain of information. Hyman, R. (1953).

name: Contrast minimum (WCAG 2.2, 1.4.3)
summary: Text needs enough contrast against its background to be read with low vision.

rule.template: Give all body text a contrast ratio of at least {minRatio} against its background.

check.selector: p, li, td, th, label, a, button, h1, h2, h3, h4, h5, h6

source: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2, Success Criterion 1.4.3.

name: Focus visible (WCAG 2.2, 2.4.7)
summary: Keyboard users must be able to see which element has focus at every moment.
when: Every screen with links, buttons or form fields.

rule.template: Show a focus outline at least {minOutlinePx} thick on every interactive element reached by keyboard.

source: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2, Success Criteria 2.4.7 (Focus Visible) and 2.4.13 (Focus Appearance).

name: Response-time limits
summary: A response within 0.1 s feels instant; after about 1 s users notice they are waiting.
when: Every control that changes something on screen when it is activated.

rule.template: Show a visible response within {maxMs} of every button press.

source: Miller, R. B. (1968). Response time in man-computer conversational transactions. Nielsen, J. (1993). Usability Engineering, chapter 5.

name: Recognition over recall
summary: Recognising an option on screen is easier than remembering it from an earlier step.
when: Multi-step forms, filters and any screen that depends on an earlier choice.

rule.template: Keep earlier choices visible on every step that depends on them.

check.question: On each later step of a multi-step form, are the choices made in earlier steps visible without going back?

source: Nielsen, J. (1994). Enhancing the explanatory power of usability heuristics. Heuristic 6: recognition rather than recall.

name: Consistency and standards (Jakob's law)
summary: Users expect the same thing to look and work the same way everywhere, as it does in products they already know.
when: Products with more than one main screen.

rule.template: Keep the main navigation in the same place and the same order on every screen.

check.question: Moving between the main screens, does the main navigation stay in the same place in the same order?

source: Nielsen, J. (1994). Heuristic 4: consistency and standards. Nielsen, J. (2000). Jakob's law of internet user experience.

name: Law of proximity (Gestalt)
summary: Things placed close together are read as one group.
when: Forms, settings and any screen with groups of related fields.

rule.template: Group related fields by spacing, with more space between groups than inside them.

check.question: On each form, is the gap between groups of fields larger than the gap between fields inside a group?

source: Wertheimer, M. (1923). Untersuchungen zur Lehre von der Gestalt II. Psychologische Forschung, 4.

name: Von Restorff effect
summary: Among similar items, the one that differs is the one people notice and remember.
when: Lists and tables where one item needs attention, such as an error or an overdue date.

rule.template: Make the item that needs attention differ by more than colour: add a word, an icon or weight.

check.question: In a list with a flagged item, such as an overdue row, can you still find that item with the screen in greyscale?

source: von Restorff, H. (1933). Psychologische Forschung, 18. W3C, WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 1.4.1 (Use of Color).

name: Help users recover from errors
summary: An error message helps only if it says what went wrong and how to put it right.
when: Every form and every action that can fail.

rule.template: Show each error next to its field, saying what went wrong and what to do next.

check.question: When a required field is left empty on submit, does the message next to that field say what to enter?

source: Nielsen, J. (1994). Heuristic 9: help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors.

name: Goal-gradient effect
summary: People speed up and drop out less when they can see how close they are to the goal.
when: Flows with three or more steps, such as checkout, booking or onboarding.

rule.template: Show the current step and the total number of steps in every multi-step flow.

check.question: On each step of a multi-step flow, does the screen show its position, such as Step 2 of 4?

source: Hull, C. L. (1932). The goal-gradient hypothesis and maze learning. Kivetz, R., Urminsky, O., Zheng, Y. (2006).

name: Peak-end rule
summary: People judge an experience mostly by its most intense moment and by its end.
when: Flows with a clear end, such as booking or sign-up.

rule.template: End every main flow on a screen that confirms the result and offers one next step.

check.question: At the end of the main flow, does the last screen say in plain words what happened and offer one next step?

source: Kahneman, D., Fredrickson, B. L., Schreiber, C. A., Redelmeier, D. A. (1993).
